youtube.title: This Photo Took Days to Take (The Oldest Camera Photo)
youtube.description:
The oldest surviving photograph made with a camera: Nicéphore Niépce's "View from the Window at Le Gras", c. 1827, made at his estate in Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, France. It is a pewter plate thinly coated with bitumen of Judea (a natural asphalt): bitumen hardens where light hits it, and the unhardened parts were washed away with oil of lavender and white petroleum.

How long was the exposure? The traditional estimate is about 8 hours; a modern researcher who recreated Niépce's process concluded it must have lasted several days — historians still differ. Either way, 8 hours = 28,800 s, about 230 million times longer than a 1/8000 s shutter.

The clue: sunlight hits the buildings on opposite sides, because the sun moved across the sky while the plate was exposed. The courtyard in this Short is our own numpy simulation (not the real photo): one instant lights one side, the whole day lights both.

Sources: Harry Ransom Center (University of Texas at Austin), which holds the heliograph; Wikipedia (View from the Window at Le Gras; Heliography; Shutter speed); Smarthistory.
